Meet the Team

We are a team of four students who came together for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to build Survive 30 Sols, our answer to the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.

1. Gurubindra Singh: Web Developer

Education: Currently pursuing a BS in Data Science and Applications at IIT Madras.

Role in the hackathon: Gurubindra led the frontend development of the website. He built the interface players see and interact with, from the Live Space Explorer to the mission screens.

2. Hritika Sharma: Backend Developer

Education: Holds a BSc degree and is currently pursuing a BS in Data Science and Applications at IIT Madras.

Role in the hackathon: Hritika developed the backend of the website and handled its deployment. She also created the team’s presentation.

3. Aayush Mishra: Research Specialist

Education: Currently pursuing a BTech in Computer Science and Engineering at Samrat Ashok Technological Institute (SATI), Vidisha.

Role in the hackathon: Aayush collected and organized the data from NASA and other space agencies that powers the game. He also led the AI integration.

4. Lohit Kumar Gorh: Research Specialist and Game Designer

Education: Currently pursuing a BTech in Electronics and Communication Engineering at Gurukul Kangri (Deemed to be University), Haridwar.

Role in the hackathon: Lohit designed the game and created its graphics using Blender and AI tools. He also kept detailed records of the project and cross-checked every figure against real space data.
summary:
Survive 30 Sols is a freely accessible, turn-based simulation in which students aged 10–15 command an extraterrestrial outpost on the Moon or Mars and must sustain a four-person crew for 30 days. Each sol they apportion a finite power budget among life support, hydroponic food production, radiation shielding, and scientific research and maintenance, then confront contingencies derived from authentic NASA missions, such as the 2018 Martian dust storm.

It addresses the challenge by transforming abstract engineering trade-offs into consequential decisions with immediate, observable repercussions. Every parameter is grounded in NASA data, and a counterfactual debrief re-simulates the mission to isolate the pivotal decision that preserved or doomed it.

Its significance lies in experiential learning: students internalise why missions succeed or fail by exercising judgement under constraint, not by passively reading. A mission lasts 10–15 minutes and runs in any browser without registration, making it readily deployable in classrooms.
details:
What it does and how it works

Survive 30 Sols is a turn-based web game for students aged 10–15. The player commands an outpost on the Moon (south pole) or Mars (Jezero Crater) and must keep a crew of four alive for 30 sols.

  • Explore: the site opens on a Live Space Explorer with six 3D views (galaxy, solar system, Earth orbit, asteroids, Moon, Mars). It shows live satellites from CelesTrak, asteroid close approaches from NASA NeoWs, and planet positions computed from JPL orbital elements.
  • Choose: a 3D Mission Dashboard where the player picks a world and one of four difficulty levels: Cadet, Astronaut, Commander, or Live NASA, which is set by the Sun’s real activity over the last 30 days (NASA DONKI).
  • Daily loop: a briefing from Nova, the CAPCOM; splitting one power budget between life support, greenhouse, shielding, and science and repair; one action (Build, Repair, Plant, Explore or Shelter); an event card based on a real NASA mission with a “Why?” explanation; then a night report.
  • Debrief: the game replays the mission about 4,000 times, changing one choice each time, and shows the single decision that mattered most, plus a sol-by-sol chart and a star rating.
  • Extras: a 3D base that reflects the game state, a first-person EVA with real gravity, a rover, a rock scanner, three junior astronauts to command, a walk-in habitat, guided tours, a teacher page and a help centre.

Benefits

  • Free, no login and no install; runs on phones, laptops and Chromebooks.
  • One mission takes 10–15 minutes, so it fits into a lesson.
  • Every number is sourced and listed in the game for teachers to check.
  • Works offline-safe: if live feeds fail, it falls back to estimates and says so.
  • Weapon-free, with plain language.

Intended impact

Students learn why missions succeed or fail by making the engineering trade-offs themselves: margins, backups, energy storage and shielding. The aim is to build systems thinking and interest in space careers.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: JavaScript (JSX), HTML, CSS, SQL, and TypeScript for the email function.
  • Front end: React 19 and Vite.
  • 3D and charts: three.js (PBR materials, post-processing, adaptive quality) and Chart.js.
  • Orbits: satellite.js (SGP4).
  • Sound: Web Audio, synthesised in the browser, plus browser text-to-speech for Nova.
  • Back end: Supabase (Postgres with row-level security, an Edge Function, Resend email) for support tickets and feedback.
  • Testing and hosting: Vitest and a 1,000-game balance simulator; deployed on Netlify.
  • Data and assets: NASA DONKI, NeoWs, Mars24, BVAD, Planetary Fact Sheets and NASA 3D models (Perseverance, Ingenuity); JPL elements; CelesTrak.
  • Hardware: none beyond a standard computer.
  • AI disclosure: an AI coding assistant helped draft code and text; all numbers were checked against NASA and peer-reviewed sources. No live AI runs during play.

How it is creative

  • The debrief names the exact decision that saved or ended the mission.
  • Difficulty is driven by real space weather.
  • Every data card carries a badge saying how live it is (live, last known, computed now, estimate).
  • The 3D base changes with the player’s choices: the shield mound grows, plants mature, dust storms darken the sky.
  • The Moon is silent because there is no air to carry sound.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific accuracy: NASA values are kept separate from game-design choices, which are labelled as such.
  • Age fit: four systems and three crew meters, so it is neither oversimplified nor too complex.
  • Balance: a first-try player wins about 41% of missions on the standard level.
  • Accessibility: touch controls, a reduce-motion option and optional voice.
  • Performance: automatic graphics presets for low-end devices.
  • Privacy: no accounts; progress is saved only in the browser.
  • Classroom use: short sessions, a teacher page, and API caching for many students at once.
